title: Merton, again
tomorrow: God asks Adam a question in a garden. what is it, and why ask?

lines: A NEW NAME AND A UNIFORM?
cards: Every app wants a profile: the best photo, a clever bio, the version of you that gets the likes. A monk in Kentucky had a name for that version.
He called it the false self, a mask we build for the world and then forget we're wearing. Here's the strange part.

To find the face underneath, he took a new name, put on the same robe as every other monk in the house, and kept the same daily schedule as all of them. Then he wrote that for him, being a saint means being himself.
A new name and a uniform, to become yourself? That sounds backwards.

teach.b: He's Thomas Merton, a writer who became a Trappist monk at the Abbey of Gethsemani, called Father Louis inside the walls. The puzzle solves like this.
The false self, he wrote, is the one we assemble out of what others see: the highlight reel, the reputation, the image we polish and defend. It feels solid, but it's a costume.

teach.h: THE TRUE SELF: THE ONE GOD SEES.
teach.b: The true self is the person God sees and loves, hidden under all that, sometimes unknown even to us. So the robe and the new name weren't a disguise.
They were a way of taking the costume off: no brand, nothing to perform. He used a tree to explain it.
A tree, he said, gives glory to God by being a tree, not by trying to be something else.
Holiness, in his telling, isn't becoming a copy of some other saint. It's becoming the one person God had in mind.
Underneath sits a line from Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims: "to the image of God he created him." Something to tell a friend tonight: Merton's own mask-dropping moment didn't happen in a chapel.
It happened on a busy street corner in Louisville, where he suddenly saw the strangers around him shining, and knew he loved them.

how: Catholics read Merton's books on prayer and contemplation in parishes, retreat houses and study groups; Trappist monasteries like Gethsemani welcome retreat guests for silent prayer.

o: a monk who wrote that the self must be erased
a monk who wrote that holiness is being yourself
a poet who wrote about life on the open road

games.q: the monk and his puzzle — tap the pairs.
p: the costume we polish and defend
the person God sees and loves
gives glory by being a tree

s: Merton taught that holiness means copying some other saint
he said it means becoming the one person God had in mind.
Merton's moment of love for strangers came on a city street
a busy corner in Louisville, not a chapel.
for Merton, the 'false self' means your body or your feelings
it's the image we build for others to see: the costume, not the person.

games.q: at a family party your cousin keeps changing how she talks depending on who's in the room, and she's exhausted. what would Merton point her toward?
o: the self under the roles, the one God sees, who doesn't have to perform.
a better mask: pick one version of herself and keep it everywhere.
leaving parties for good, since holiness means hiding from people.
games.why: Merton's way out of the false self wasn't hiding: his own big moment was loving strangers on a busy Louisville street.

practice: Sit the way you sit when nobody's watching: not posed, not slumped for show. Open your hands on your knees with nothing in them, no phone and no role.
For the sit, just be the person who is here, and if you pray, let God look at that one, no mask.

wordCard.voice: Merton. Thomas Merton, a Trappist monk and writer who said holiness means becoming your true self, the one God sees.

orig.note: Latin, Genesis 1:27 in the Vulgate: to the image of God, the dignity under every mask.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: true self, the face under the costume, the one God already sees. Until tomorrow.
